t: Find the Minimum Cost Array Permutation — Bitmask DP with Lexicographic Reconstruction
o: score(perm) is a cycle of edges: edge from a to b costs |a − nums[b]|, wrapping from the last element back to the first. Rotating a permutation doesn't change the score, so some optimal permutation starts with 0 — fixing perm[0] = 0 is safe and also yields the lexicographically smallest representative. With n ≤ 14, Held–Karp bitmask DP applies: g[mask][last] = minimum cost to complete the cycle given the visited set mask (containing 0 and last) and current node last. Example 1: [0,1,2] achieves cost 2; example 2: [0,2,1] achieves 2.
k: Cycle score is rotation-invariant ⇒ fix perm[0] = 0 without loss.
Held–Karp DP over (visited subset, last node) with O(2ⁿ·n²) transitions.
Lexicographic tie-break: reconstruct greedily, always trying the smallest next index whose completion cost matches the DP optimum.

a.n: Approach 1: Bitmask DP + Greedy Path Reconstruction
a.i: Compute g[mask][last] backwards: g[full][last] = |last − nums[0]| (closing edge); otherwise g[mask][last] = min over unvisited nxt of |last − nums[nxt]| + g[mask ∪ nxt][nxt]. The answer is g[{0}][0]. To get the lexicographically smallest optimum, walk forward from state ({0}, 0), at each step choosing the smallest nxt such that the edge cost plus g of the successor state equals the current state's value — this provably follows one optimal, lex-smallest tour.
s: Allocate g[(1<<n)][n]; fill masks in decreasing order.
Base: g[FULL][last] = |last − nums[0]| for last in mask.
Transition: g[mask][last] = min over nxt ∉ mask of |last − nums[nxt]| + g[mask | 1<<nxt][nxt].
Reconstruct from (1, 0) by scanning nxt ascending and matching values; prepend 0 and return.
a.t: O(2ⁿ·n²) — each of the 2ⁿ·n states relaxes up to n successors; n ≤ 14 gives ~3.2M operations.
a.sp: O(2ⁿ·n) — the DP table (about 229K integers for n = 14).

w: Two insights carry the solution: rotational symmetry lets you pin perm[0] = 0 (halving confusion and guaranteeing lex-smallestness), and the greedy reconstruction over ascending candidates yields the lexicographic tie-break for free. Pitfalls: forgetting the wrap-around edge |perm[n−1] − nums[perm[0]]| in the base case, and skipping masks that don't contain node 0. Follow-up: return the score itself, or handle n up to 20 (still bitmask DP but memory-tighter with hash maps).
